content: A parasitic plant is a type of plant that obtains some or all of its nutrients from another plant. Approximately 4,100 species of parasitic plants exist, distributed across 19 families of flowering plants. These plants possess a specialized structure called a haustorium, which is a modified root that penetrates the host plant and connects to its vascular system, such as the xylem, phloem, or both. Parasitic plants can be classified into several categories based on their dependency on the host, the part of the host they attach to, and their ability to photosynthesize: 1. Obligate parasites are entirely dependent on a host plant to complete their life cycle. 2. Facultative parasites can complete their life cycle without a host but may parasitize other plants under certain conditions. 3. Stem parasites attach to the stems of their host plants. 4. Root parasites attach to the roots of their host plants. 5. Holoparasites are completely parasitic and lack significant amounts of chlorophyll, meaning they do not perform photosynthesis. 6. Hemiparasites are partially parasitic and retain some ability to photosynthesize. Hemiparasites may extract water and minerals from their host plants, and many also obtain organic nutrients from their hosts. Examples of parasitic plants include: Nuytsia floribunda (Western Australian Christmas tree), which is an obligate root hemiparasite. Rhinanthus (Yellow rattle), which is a facultative root hemiparasite. Mistletoe, which is an obligate stem hemiparasite. Dodder (Cuscuta spp.), which is a stem holoparasite. Hydnora species, which are root holoparasites. Holoparasites are always obligate parasites, meaning they cannot survive without a host. Examples of holoparasitic plants include broomrape (Orobanche), dodder (Cuscuta), Rafflesia, and members of the family Hydnoraceae. Hemiparasitic plants include Castilleja (Indian paintbrush), mistletoe, the Western Australian Christmas tree, and yellow rattle. Specific examples of holoparasites include Hyobanche sanguinea, which is found in regions such as Richtersveld and Goegap Nature Reserve in Namaqualand, Northern Cape, South Africa. Host Range Parasitic plants exhibit varying degrees of host specificity. Some are generalists, parasitizing multiple species, sometimes even simultaneously. For instance, dodder (Cuscuta spp. and Cassytha spp.) and red rattle (Odontites verna) are generalist parasites. Others are specialists, targeting only a few or even a single species. For example, beech drops (Epifagus virginiana) is a root holoparasite that exclusively parasitizes American beech (Fagus grandifolia), while Rafflesia parasitizes the vine Tetrastigma. Importance Parasitic plants have significant ecological, economic, and cultural importance: Agricultural pests such as witchweed (Striga), broomrape (Orobanche), and dodder (Cuscuta) cause substantial economic losses in herbaceous crops. Mistletoes can damage forest and ornamental trees, though they are also culturally significant as a Christmas decoration, associated with the tradition of kissing under the mistletoe. Rafflesia arnoldii produces the largest flowers in the world, measuring about one meter in diameter, and serves as a major tourist attraction in its native habitat. The Indian paintbrush (Castilleja linariaefolia) is the state flower of Wyoming, while the oak mistletoe (Phoradendron serotinum) is the state flower of Oklahoma. Some parasitic plants, such as Nuytsia and broomrape, are occasionally cultivated for their ornamental flowers. Parasitic plants are valuable in scientific research, particularly in studies on the evolutionary loss of photosynthesis. A few parasitic plants have been used as food by humans. The Western Australian Christmas tree (Nuytsia floribunda) has been known to damage underground cables, mistaking them for host roots and attempting to parasitize them using its specialized guillotine-like structures. Plants Parasitic on Fungi Approximately 400 species of flowering plants and one gymnosperm (Parasitaxus usta) are parasitic on mycorrhizal fungi. These plants are referred to as myco-heterotrophs rather than parasitic plants. Examples of myco-heterotrophs include: Indian pipe (Monotropa uniflora), Snow plant (Sarcodes sanguinea), Underground orchid (Rhizanthella gardneri), Bird's nest orchid (Neottia nidus-avis), and Sugarstick (Allotropa virgata).
